When "divine" is used as a noun, it refers to a person of the clergy or a theologian — someone who has dedicated their life to the study, teaching, or practice of religious faith. In plain terms: a priest, a minister, a pastor, or a religious scholar who is deeply learned in theology (the study of God and religious belief).

Think of it this way: just as a native can mean a person who belongs to a place, a divine means a person who belongs to — or serves — the domain of God and religion.

"The divines of the church gathered to settle the dispute over scripture."

Here, "divines" simply means a group of learned clergy or theologians.

This is a formal and somewhat old-fashioned word. You won't hear it in everyday conversation today, but you will encounter it frequently in historical texts, literature, philosophy, and religious writings — especially from the 16th to 19th centuries. For example, the famous "Westminster Assembly of Divines" (1643) was a gathering of theologians convened to reform the English church.

There is a second, distinct usage of "divine" as a noun — when it appears as "the Divine" (usually capitalized, always with the). Here, it does not refer to a person. Instead, it refers to God, or the quality of being God, or the sacred spiritual power that underlies all existence.

This usage is abstract and philosophical. It captures the idea of the supreme, the holy, the infinite — whatever a person or tradition considers to be the ultimate spiritual reality.

"Artists have long tried to capture the Divine in their work."
"She felt a deep yearning to connect with the Divine."
"Many philosophers have argued about the nature of the Divine."

Notice that in this usage, "the Divine" stands in for something vast and sacred — it is a way of talking about God or ultimate holiness without naming any specific religion or deity. It is often preferred in philosophical, mystical, or interfaith contexts precisely because it is broad and non-sectarian.
Two Distinct Usages, Side by Side

To keep it clear in your mind:

  • "A divine" / "the divines" → a person (a clergyman or theologian). Countable. Old-fashioned.
  • "The Divine" → an abstract idea (God, the sacred, the holy). Uncountable. Still in active use in philosophy, spirituality, and literature.

"A divine" (meaning a clergy member or theologian) appears almost exclusively in:

  • Historical writing and documents
  • Classic English literature (Shakespeare's era through the Victorian era)
  • Academic writing about religion and history

You would not call a modern priest "a divine" in casual speech — it would sound archaic. But if you're reading older texts or writing in a formal, literary style, it fits perfectly.

"The Divine" (meaning God or the sacred) is alive and well today. You'll find it in:

  • Philosophy of religion
  • Mystical and spiritual writing (across many traditions — Christian, Hindu, Sufi, New Age, etc.)
  • Poetry and literary prose
  • Interfaith dialogue, where a neutral term for the sacred is useful

Both uses of "divine" as a noun share the same root idea: something — or someone — connected to God or to the highest spiritual reality. Whether it is a theologian who spends his life studying God ("a divine"), or the infinite sacred presence itself ("the Divine"), the word always carries a sense of the holy, the elevated, and the transcendent.

If you ever see "divine" in a text and you're unsure which meaning applies, ask yourself: Is it referring to a person, or to an abstract spiritual idea? That distinction will always guide you to the right meaning.
